extracted.intended_audience: general readers; students and scholars of literature; creative writers interested in Achebe's style and African literature
extracted.subtask_description: Analyse the features, techniques, themes, and cultural commitments of Chinua Achebe's fiction and non-fiction as described in the Wikipedia article; useful for writers and students learning from Achebe's approach. Focuses on stylistic devices (oral tradition, proverbs, narration), thematic concerns (colonialism, culture, politics), and professional practices (editing, publishing, advocacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Draw on the oral tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe's fiction 'draws heavily on the oral tradition of the Igbo people.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Incorporate folk tales, songs, myths and other oral forms into both content and form so that community values are exposed through storytelling techniques; use oral-material devices (masquerade ceremonies, communal tales) to ground fiction in indigenous cultural practice. Example: the tale about the Earth and Sky in Things Fall Apart emphasises interdependency of masculine and feminine.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use proverbs as structural and thematic devices
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe 'used proverbs to describe the values' of his culture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Employ proverbs and succinct aphorisms to convey communal wisdom, character viewpoints, and moral tensions; let characters' reactions to proverbs reveal cultural conflicts (e.g., Okonkwo's dislike for a mother's tale shows imbalance). Proverbs can function as concentrated ethical shading and help preserve local voice within English prose.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine straightforward narration with representations of folk stories and oratory
rubrics_metrics.description: His style 'combines straightforward narration with representations of folk stories, proverbs, and oratory.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a clear, unadorned narrative voice while weaving in embedded oral-material passages; balance lucidity and accessibility with culturally specific, performative elements so that narrative remains readable yet rooted in local forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write realistic dialogue by mastering spoken-language nuance
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe's radio work 'helped him master the subtle nuances between written and spoken language, a skill that helped him later to write realistic dialogue.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop ear for spoken idiom and rhythm—use experience with oral/performative delivery (scripts, readings) to craft dialogue that captures speech patterns, register shifts, and communal modes of address; test dialogue aloud or via oral-delivery exercises.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use English as a vehicle while preserving indigenous perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe 'wrote in and defended the use of English, describing it as a means to reach a broad audience,' while drawing on Igbo traditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing in a colonial/global lingua franca, adapt the language to carry local cadence, imagery and worldview rather than adopting an external/colonial voice; use syntax, idioms, and narrative priorities that foreground indigenous outlooks while maintaining intelligibility for wider audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Center themes on culture, colonialism, gender, politics, and history
rubrics_metrics.description: Among the many themes his works cover are culture and colonialism, masculinity and femininity, politics, and history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Deliberately engage with the intersections of tradition and colonial modernity: examine how political structures, gender roles, and historical change shape individual and communal lives; use fiction to interrogate cultural encounter and power relations rather than merely ornamenting plot.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray characters within communal contexts rather than purely individualistic frameworks
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe suggested that the 'individualistic hero was rare in African literature, given its roots in communal living' and characters are 'subject to non-human forces in the universe.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop characters whose motivations, failures, and identities are embedded in community, tradition, ritual, and metaphysical forces; avoid privileging hyper-individualism when representing societies where communal bonds and obligations structure action and meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blend myth, legend and modern styles
rubrics_metrics.description: Works like Anthills of the Savannah offer 'a powerful fusion of myth, legend and modern styles.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fuse mythic or legendary materials with contemporary narrative techniques—use allegory, symbolic figures, and communal myths alongside modern forms (satire, realist plot) to create layering and depth; ensure the blend serves thematic purpose rather than feeling decorative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exercise editorial rigor and structural focus
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe revised and restructured Things Fall Apart—'He cut away the second and third sections of the book, leaving only the story... He added sections, improved various chapters, and restructured the prose.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be willing to excise entire sections and reshape structure for focus; concentrate the narrative on its central arc and themes, trimming material that distracts from the work's core. Use rigorous revision to strengthen voice and clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read and critique canonical Western texts from an informed postcolonial perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: In essays such as 'An Image of Africa: Racism in Conrad's Heart of Darkness' Achebe argued that Conrad's novel 'dehumanises Africans' and reframed Western portrayals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Approach established Western texts critically—re-evaluate their representations of other cultures, and position new work in dialogue with (not merely imitation of) those canons. Encourage comparative reading ('read it beside African works') to reveal blind spots and open alternative interpretive frames.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match form to context: use shorter, intense forms in crisis
rubrics_metrics.description: During the Nigerian Civil War Achebe wrote mostly poetry: 'The shorter format was a consequence of living in a war zone. "I can write poetry, something short, intense more in keeping with my mood..."'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select literary form according to emotional and material circumstances—shorter, intense forms (poems, short stories) may better capture urgency, fragmentation, or constrained conditions; be flexible in choosing form to suit mood and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Act as cultural advocate, editor and mentor to build literary community
rubrics_metrics.description: Achebe helped found and edit the African Writers Series and recommended and promoted other African writers (Ngũgĩ wa Thiong'o, Flora Nwapa), and served as an editor and publisher.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond individual composition, contribute to literary ecosystems: edit, mentor, advocate for publishing avenues that amplify marginalized voices; curatorial and institutional work (series, journals) is a part of sustaining a national/regional literature.
